All eyes on the EU as UK bans imports from Israeli settlements
item.description:
Britain's decision this week to ban all imports from illegal Israeli settlements carries huge moral resonance, but the real test comes next: Will the European Union (EU) – the single largest market in the world and Israel's biggest trading partner – follow suit?

The EU conducts trade worth tens of billions with Israel every year, but it has long hidden behind the need for consensus or the lack of a majority required to use its massive economic leverage to influence Israel's policies.

The key question is whether the UK's decision will act as a catalyst and sway a sufficient number of European governments to act.

The timing is critical. Last month, the Israeli government called for tenders to build more than 1,200 housing units in E1 – a 4.6 square mile area in the occupied West Bank that lies between Jerusalem and the large Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim. Any such expansion would make a “contiguous Palestinian state virtually impossible,” as CNN reported last month.

The EU has two options. It could find the unity needed to exert influence now, before Israel starts the construction and changes facts on the ground that later become difficult to reverse. Or it could squander the possibility of a two-state solution.

In a speech at the House of Commons, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband delivered a scathing admonishment of the Israeli government, accusing it of turning a blind eye to the "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians" perpetrated by "settler terrorists" in the West Bank.

Miliband cited United Nations reporting of an "average of six violent settler attacks against Palestinians per day this year, the highest on record."

Settlement trade mostly consists of agricultural products and, as Reuters reported, represents only a fraction of the total bilateral trade between the UK and Israel. The UK's sanctions on companies and individuals that facilitate settlement expansion – including financial institutions – could prove to be more impactful. Israel’s banks and insurance companies that back construction projects in illegal settlements may think twice before risking their business interests in the UK.

Yet, despite a scathing denouncement and a seemingly sweeping sanctions package, there is only so much the UK can do alone.

The EU – a 27-member bloc of some of the most prosperous nations in the world – has much greater leverage.

Last year, the EU and Israel traded more than €43 billion in goods. The popular debate has been about reducing arms sales to Israel, but Europe's real power is economic; using trade as leverage would offer a genuine chance of making the Israeli establishment rethink its settlement expansion and policies in occupied territories at large.

Miliband said the UK coordinated with 11 other countries, including France and Canada, and shortly after, Paris announced that it will impose a ban on all imports from illegal settlements. Canada's foreign minister, Anita Anand, promised the introduction of "restrictions" in the coming months. Nine other states – Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, and Sweden – expressed their intention to introduce national restrictions, support European restrictions, or at least "actively consider" a ban on trade in goods with settlements and other measures.

The extent to which these countries will go against Israel remains unclear, but they need more countries to come on board for it to be a pan-European ban.

There is no doubt that European countries have disapproved of Israeli methods and mass killings in Gaza and, lately, the exacerbation of settler violence in the West Bank. But the bloc as a whole has failed to turn its concern into a coherent policy that has an effect on the ground.

Over the last three years, the EU and its member states have discussed several proposals about how they can persuade Israel to rein in its military campaign, send more aid to Gaza, and control the violent settlers unleashing havoc in the West Bank.

Last year, the EU conducted a review of the EU-Israel Association Agreement, which provides the legal framework for economic and political relations. It later found Israel in breach of Article 2 of the treaty, which identifies respect for human rights and democratic principles as "essential elements."

The EU leaders then discussed a slew of options, including fully suspending the agreement, but this required unanimity to push through and was never seriously considered. Under Viktor Orbán, Hungary was one of the principal opponents of suspending the EU–Israel Association Agreement, effectively blocking the unanimity required. (Hungary's new leader, Peter Magyar, has not joined the new national initiative but has been more willing to support EU action against Israel. This May, Hungary backed EU sanctions against some extremist settlers and entities.)

The other option was a partial suspension of trade-related provisions, which required a qualified majority vote (QMV) – at least 15 affirmative votes representing 65% of the bloc's population. While Hungary was a convenient scapegoat, Germany's support for Israel, alongside Italy's, held back the bloc from moving forward.

Suspending Israel's participation in the Erasmus+ student exchange programme or the Horizon academic research programme was also tabled. At the time, a senior EU official told me these were the "low-hanging fruit" and doable, but nothing moved forward.

Some options were outside the scope of the association agreement – including halting visa-free travel for Israelis to the EU and banning imports from illegal Israeli settlements.

According to an EU spokesperson, as of last week, the bloc had sanctioned a dozen individuals and nine entities related to illegal settlements, but there was no "clear outcome" to the discussions about other options on the table. He presumably meant a ban on imports from the settlements.

This week, in a candid conversation, a senior EU official told me that the European Commission had later tabled a new proposal, specifically laying out options to deter Israel from expanding illegal settlements, including the ban on imports, but not even 15 member states are on board.

In short, the EU has long discussed a hierarchy of possible measures, from the least to the most consequential, but has dithered on moving forward. It has a chance now, if it wants to stop Israel from expanding E1. If consensus and QMV cripple the EU from moving ahead as a bloc, the least European nations can do is take national measures.

Will they?

Trade in goods between the EU and Israel favored Europeans last year. Moreover, Europeans are likely to factor in a growing dependence on Israel's defense industry as relations with the U.S. decline and the U.S. itself runs short on critical munitions. Germany, Greece, Cyprus, Finland, and many others import Israeli defense equipment.

For now, therefore, the chances of a pan-EU ban on imports from West Bank settlements remain low, and the odds of a suspension of trade with Israel are lower yet.

item.title: Can Milei count on Trump to deliver on the Falklands?
item.description:
The territorial dispute between Argentina and the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands (or Islas Malvinas in Spanish) continues to escalate.

Last week, Argentine President Javier Milei, a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, announced a series of new measures aimed at pressuring Britain over the future of the islands. The most significant announcement was of new sanctions on companies involved in oil extraction in the waters around the Falklands, which Argentina has long claimed as its own. Argentina’s attempt to prevent the exploitation of the Falklands’ natural resources is a reminder that beneath the often farcical relitigating of sovereignty claims dating back to the 18th century is a very modern geopolitical conflict with real stakes for energy and maritime resources.

Yet what was most remarkable about Milei’s announcement was what Milei did not announce — namely, a shift in U.S. policy regarding the Falklands. Given the hype that Milei built up ahead of his announcement, many observers speculated he would announce U.S. support for Argentina’s claim. Those expectations had been further raised by a steady trickle of reporting going back to April that the Trump administration has been considering recognizing Argentina’s claim to the Falklands, bolstered by Trump’s recent comment that the U.S. position on the islands was “one of many” under review.

The Falklands question, though easily dismissed as a curiosity in the United States, has long presented a genuine dilemma for U.S. policymakers torn between its transatlantic alliance and the Western Hemisphere. Despite being officially neutral in the territorial dispute, the U.S. decided to side with Britain over Argentina in the 1982 conflict, providing significant material support to the British war effort. This support caused lasting damage to U.S. standing in Latin America. Now, geopolitical shifts in the United States, Europe and Latin America have all converged to Argentina’s advantage, and help explain why Milei sees an opportunity to push Britain over the Falklands without risking broader diplomatic isolation.

It’s time to ask: what would it take to get Donald Trump to give Milei what he so clearly wants?

Milei’s self-proclaimed ability to obtain U.S. support for Argentina’s claim has become a major part of Milei’s domestic pitch. As is often noted in Argentina, Milei’s recent focus on the Falklands is a new development. Milei had risen to power with bitter and divisive attacks on left-wing domestic opponents, whom the president blamed for Argentina’s economic problems. Milei’s belated embrace of the Falklands issue comes as his economic reforms have largely failed to deliver the widespread prosperity he promised.

Milei’s bet is that close alignment with the U.S. will translate to U.S. support for Argentina’s territorial claim, reversing the recent pattern of Argentine diplomacy, which searched for allies in the Global South. In this effort, Milei may well be repeating the error of the Argentine military junta, which believed the U.S. would stay neutral or even support Argentina in the 1982 war over the islands. Milei is betting this time will be different.

For the United States, however, most of the recent consideration about whether to back Argentina over Britain in the South Atlantic has not revolved around the Falklands at all. For Trump, the Falklands question is clearly about Iran, with reports pointing to his notable frustration with Britain for its perceived failure to support the U.S.-Israeli war. Yet regardless of Trump’s frustration, Britain remains a far more useful ally in the current Middle Eastern conflict than Argentina could ever hope to be. British bases on Cyprus and Diego Garcia have served as logistical hubs for U.S. operations, and even briefly came under fire from Iran and its allies. While Trump no doubt wants Britain to do more, he also wouldn’t want Britain to do less.

Milei’s government has acted in lockstep with the United States on the diplomatic front, designating Iran’s IRGC a terrorist organization. Washington is clearly interested in such support, as indicated by the State Department’s trumpeting of Peru’s recent decision to break off diplomatic relations with Iran.

Yet these diplomatic “wins” are more about recognizing U.S. dominance over the Western Hemisphere than anything else; neither Peru or Argentina can make any real military contribution to the actual armed conflict. Undersecretary of Defense Elbridge Colby effectively acknowledged as much in his recent Americas Quarterly essay, writing “we will not ask neighbors to project power out of this region.” This gives Britain the upper hand for now.

Closer to home, though, the case for U.S. recognition of the Argentine claim is far more straightforward: the U.S. has a clear and permanent interest in close ties with Latin America. The Trump administration has embraced the Monroe Doctrine, the original purpose of which was to defend the newly independent states of Latin America from exactly the sort of European imperial predations that Britain accomplished by seizing the Malvinas from Argentina by threat of force in 1833. If the United States truly means to prioritize the Western Hemisphere over Europe or the Middle East, then trading Britain for Argentina makes much more sense.

The Falklands also occupy another strategic waterway — the approaches to the Strait of Magellan and Cape Horn. Before the construction of the Panama Canal (another Trump obsession), the Falklands commanded the only maritime corridor between the Pacific and Atlantic oceans. Indeed, this is why Britain seized them in the first place, as part of its global network of maritime bases from Singapore to Suez to Cape Town to Gibraltar. The Falklands’ strategic importance was proved by the 1914 Battle of the Falklands, when the Royal Navy annihilated the German East Asia Squadron as it attempted to enter the Atlantic. More recently, U.S. aircraft carriers have traveled through the Strait of Magellan, a useful practice in case the Panama Canal becomes unavailable for any reason.

Milei’s pitch to Donald Trump then seems to be this: in exchange for U.S. support against Britain, Argentina would offer unprecedented access to its South Atlantic territories to both the U.S. military and U.S. business interests. Yet there are good reasons to doubt that Milei, already increasingly unpopular domestically, can keep that promise.

Many prominent leaders on the Argentine left who vocally support confrontation with Britain nevertheless see the U.S. as a similar threat to Argentine sovereignty, specifically warning against U.S. control of Argentine naval bases in Tierra del Fuego. Argentines are undoubtedly united on the Falklands across ideological lines, but they also envision the islands and the crucial sea lanes and natural resources around them returning to Argentine sovereignty, not U.S. control. The divisive and partisan governance style of both Milei and Trump makes any long-term U.S.-Argentine partnership fragile, particularly when, as seems likely, the Argentine left returns to power.

For now, Milei seems to be waiting in vain for U.S. support. Trump has already done extraordinary political favors for Milei. From facilitating a $20 billion U.S. Treasury bailout to importing Argentine beef, Trump has done more for Milei’s political fortunes than any prior U.S. leader has for any Argentine counterpart. It is also clear that the calculus of 1982 no longer holds: Britain is militarily weaker, more diplomatically isolated, and less geopolitically relevant to U.S. security needs in 2026 than in 1982. Yet Milei still needs Trump far more than Trump needs Milei.

Milei has increasingly staked his presidency on proving that his subordination to the United States will allow him to win the Falklands, the White Whale of Argentine foreign policy. Yet Milei’s needs are not Washington’s. The U.S. has no real reason to change position as long as it can string both of its nominal allies along. That is likely what Donald Trump, who is much better at talking about deals than closing them, will do.

Trumpism is the lowest stage of imperialism. “We’re not going to invade Greenland. We’re going to buy it,” Donald Trump reportedly told the annual black-tie dinner on 1 February of the private Alfalfa Club, an assemblage of prominent Washington figures, a number of whom he had publicly humiliated, and others he was investigating or suing. “It’s never been my intention to make Greenland the 51st state. I want to make Canada the 51st state. Greenland will be the 52nd state. Venezuela can be 53rd.” The room greeted several of his remarks with dead silence. His cosplay as the Pirate King was not received as a good-humored takeoff from a Gilbert and Sullivan opera. He went on. “So many people in the room I hate,” he said in a display of honesty. “Most of you I like,” he claimed. Then, at his peak euphoria, he flew off to Mar-a-Lago to plan his attack on Iran, which took place 27 days later.

Trump’s imperialism of piracy and plunder is less of a system even than that of the earliest imperialism of 17th century privateers raiding the Spanish Main, the divine right of kings, and monarchs dividing up the spoils as favors to create their lords and earls. His schemes of aggrandizement operating by threat and force are justified by no larger rationale, nothing as exalted as “the white man’s burden”, marauding wherever and however he can to seize resources.

25 years after 9/11. Whatever happened to mass-effect terrorism?
item.description:
One remaining mystery about 9/11 is why there have been no attacks of comparable scale since. But, with the combination of new motivations, enhanced means of delivery and AI -devised payloads there should be no cause for complacency.

9/11 changed everything. It led to two decades when the United States and much of Europe became fixated on Islamism. Western strategists became fluent about half absorbed subjects such as Wahhabism, Pashtun tribal customs, Frontier Crimes Regulations, and the Anbar Awakening while giving insufficient attention to Chinese economic dominance and Russian military rearmament[1]. Who knows what that diversion of strategic and intellectual resources (and the chaos it left behind in the region) has cost the West?

9/11 also bookends that remarkable period from the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1989/90 when peace and reconciliation seemed to break out everywhere. The Oslo Accords of 1993 seemed to chart a trajectory towards a two-state solution in Israel/Palestine. One year later the peaceful multi-party elections in South Africa were nothing short of a miracle. For years Afrikaners had insisted they would fight black rule until the last drop of white blood. This was the brief ‘unipolar moment’ under the (then) benign supervision of Washington.

9/11 ushered in a new world; one with which Thomas Hobbes would be all too familiar. “Covenants, without the sword, are but words and of no strength to secure a man at all.” “Force and fraud are in war the two cardinal virtues.” Leviathan could be quoted endlessly. .[2]

Of course, first and foremost, 9/11was a tragedy for the victims and their families. It was an act of appalling savagery. It was not only the largest terrorist attack in history by a country mile but it also introduced a new concept of mass-effect terrorism.

From the terrorists’ point of view it was also an attack of breathtaking scale and ambition. Osama Bin Laden had the imagination to view an aircraft full of fuel and passengers as a terror weapon by knitting together two of Al Qaida’s (AQ) previous failures; the truck-bomb attack on the World Trade Centre in 1993 and the 1995 Operation BOJINKA in the Philippines. Both attacks had been planned by Ramzi Yousef whose uncle Khalid Sheikh Mohammed was the chief planner for 9/11.

It was also, from an AQ viewpoint, both triumphant and disastrous. Its success was that a superpower overreacted for two decades and allowed 9/11 to shape the whole of Western foreign policy as a Global War on Terror (GWOT). Its failure was due to Washington’s largely successful determination to destroy AQ, a success which was only imperilled when President Trump approved the feckless Doha Accords with the Taliban in 2020 opening the way to the return of AQ to Afghanistan the following year. The latest United Nations report on terrorism confirms that AQ continues to reestablish itself.[3]

As early as 1998 the British government had warned Washington that it was the likely next target in an operation which would involve hijacked aircraft. This story was told in detail by RUSI for the twentieth anniversary of 9/11.[4] The intelligence was briefed to both Presidents Clinton and Bush (junior). Contrary to widespread opinion the concept of mass-effect terrorism had been exercising minds in Washington and Whitehall long before 9/11. If they had not made the intellectual leap of imagining airliners as weapons, they had nonetheless been thinking a great deal about mass casualty attacks. This was prompted by three convergent factors.

First, in Tokyo a doomsday cult known as Aum Shinrikyo had, in 1995, released sarin on the Tokyo metro in an attack which (had it been carried out more effectively) could have killed thousands. This led to much discussion of how to react to a similar attack on the London Underground. There was also concern about CBW elements being brought into the country inside the diplomatic mail bags of state sponsors of terrorism (the bags being protected from scrutiny by the Vienna Convention of 1961).[5]

Secondly there were fears at the time about Al Qaida getting its hands on nuclear material and producing a dirty bomb (not a nuclear explosion). At the time it was believed that fissile material was being sold by former employees of Soviet nuclear programme and finding its way through Central Asia to Pakistan. Most of it was a scam called ‘red mercury’ which was thoroughly investigated at the time but there were enough more credible reports to create uncertainty[6].

And finally it was known that AQ had two scientists working on CBN (chemical, biological and nuclear) experiments out of Derunta camp near the Afghan/Pakistan border. Not all the fine detail was known but one of the scientists, Dr. Sultan Bashiruddin Mahmood, had previously worked on Pakistan’s own sovereign nuclear programme. This story was well-told a decade later by the veteran journalist Peter Bergen[7].

Thus began a decade long United States fixation with the danger of terrorists obtaining access to Pakistan’s nuclear weapons. President Obama insisted that ‘The single biggest threat to U.S. security, both short term, medium term and long term, would be the possibility of a terrorist organization obtaining a nuclear weapon.’[8]

Once 9/11 had happened the assumption was that there would be numerous copy-cat attacks. In London much focus was devoted to the towers at Canary Wharf which housed some of the world’s premier financial institutions and which were also close to the flight paths of both London Heathrow and London City airport.

In the years immediately after 9/11 terrorist ambitions remained high including the Bali bombing in 2002 (202 killed), the Madrid train bombings in 2004 (193) and London 2005 (52). There were some dangerous plots in UK notably CREVICE in 2003 and RHYME in 2004 but the only one on the scale of 9/11 was Operation OVERT in 2006, AQ’s plan to bring down seven airliners in mid Atlantic. Fortunately it was thwarted by MI5.

And herein lies the real mystery. There have been numerous nasty and costly terrorist attacks since but none on the 9/11 scale. There is a danger of sounding callous when observing that none of Mumbai in 2008 (166 killed), Paris in 2015 (130), Sri Lanka 2019 (269) come even close to 9/11 (2,976).[9]

Two types of terrorism have emerged since OVERT in 2006.

The first was ‘urban siege’, ‘swarm’ or ‘rampaging’ terrorism which we first saw at Mumbai in 2008[10] and the Westgate shopping mall in Nairobi in 2013 (which killed 71). This is an effective form of terrorism because it captures press attention for hours (62 hours in the case of Mumbai) and makes prompt armed response extremely difficult. However it is also costly for the terrorists who are nearly always killed or captured and their supporting organisations and states identified. The Indians were relentlessly successful in following up the Mumbai attack although the Lashkar-e-Tayyiba still exists and represent a significant threat to regional peace.[11]

The second (and now the most common) is ‘lone wolf’ terrorism committed usually by lone (and lonely) young men who have become self-radicalised online in their bedrooms and take the family car or a kitchen knife and seek to kill as many people as possible. The problem with this second type is that it is almost indistinguishable from wider mental health problems brought about by social isolation. It risks a substantial drain on the precious resources of security services which need to be focussing on strategic threats (such as those posed by Russia, Iran and China as well as terrorist groups).

In terms of mass casualties only one is comparable with 9/11; the brutal Hamas incursion into southern Israel on 7th October 2023. As a proportion of Israel’s population it is probably the most lethal terrorist attack in history. But there the comparison ends. The attack involved guns, knives and grenades; a far cry from the use of aircraft as a weapon against a ground-based target.

Aircraft and their passengers have often been targets before, notably PanAm 103 at Lockerbie in 1988 (270 deaths), UTA flight 772 the following year over Niger (170) and the often-forgotten Air India flight 182 off the Irish coast in 1985 (329)[12]. But in each case the aircraft and passengers were the target rather than the means of delivery against an objective on the ground. 25 years after 9/11 one would have expected to have seen several similar attacks using aircraft against buildings or (even worse) against stadiums full of spectators.

Why has this not happened?

Precautions taken by airlines should take some credit. Cockpit doors have been strengthened and protocols have been largely enforced although there are signs of laxness creeping back in.

Security services have used bulk data to identify suspicious trends and plots early. Artificial Intelligence will help here. It is now much harder for terrorists to operate as groups.

And the US military, their intelligence services and allies wreaked considerable damage on both AQ and Islamic State (IS) from 2001 through until 2019.

So was 9/11 a one off rather than (as we feared) the start of a new trend? It is still too early to say. Motivation for terrorism remains strong (especially following the destruction of Gaza since October 2023). The advances in drone technology in Ukraine since 2022 could provide terrorists with an effective means of delivery at a time when counter-measures are still in their infancy. And AI could enable terrorists to research and develop lethal payloads.

As we remember 9/11 it is still too early to elcome the absence of a successful repeat during that costly quarter century. [13]

item.title: The Battle for Decision Autonomy, The New Front in Strategic Competition
item.description:
This is the talk Dave Pitts gave at the Sarajevo Security Conference in September 2026, which was based on the talk presented at the Cognitive Security Institute Conference in August 2026. Dave has identified Decision Autonomy as a key battle in the cognitive domain and a new front in strategic competition.

In 2022, Russia expected Ukraine’s political leadership to fracture in the face of pervasive disinformation, subversion, efforts to decapitate the government and to persuade Russian-speaking Ukrainians to support Russia. It expected fear, confusion, and chaos to result in surrender, flight, or capitulation. There was one problem—Ukraine resisted.

President Zelensky's refusal to flee, combined with unified military and civilian resistance—critical decisions—enabled Ukraine to hold in those critical early hours and days. How did such a small number of people resist such extraordinary pressure and make such consequential decisions?

In 2024, a mature Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall, a major producer of artillery shells for Ukraine, was discovered and disrupted by German and Western intelligence. More recently, German reporting described a suspected Russian-linked plot against Stefan Thumann of Donaustahl, a German drone producer supporting Ukraine.

What could those plots have achieved if successful? What did they actually achieve?

Russian drone incursions, airspace violations, political interference, cyberattacks, undersea cable cutting, GPS jamming, forced migration, sabotage, assassination, and attacks on critical infrastructure—several things have become increasingly clear. Russia’s gray zone attacks have increased since it invaded Ukraine. They have become more brazen, more lethal and more destructive—and spread across an increasing number of European countries.

The real question behind these attacks is why Russia is doing this. There are some obvious answers, but do we have it right?

America directly—and many countries indirectly—face a strategic challenge in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s attempts to control the flow of vital global energy as leverage in its conflict with the United States and Israel have created a wicked strategic decision point. Iran’s concurrent attacks on its neighbors may also serve as decision accelerants, compressing the time available to assess options and increasing pressure to act.

What decisions are possible and potentially effective? What are the risks and consequences of each option? And, perhaps most importantly, how much influence over that decision does Iran have?

No single human capacity is more powerful—or more vulnerable—than the ability to make decisions. Throughout history and continuing today, human decision-making has remained a target of those who seek to control the choices of others.

The ability—and the autonomy—to make decisions, from the ordinary choices of everyday life to the most consequential decisions of war and peace, makes us uniquely human. We instinctively resist—and, if necessary, fight—as individuals, groups, and nations when others seek to control our choices, think for us, or suppress this core human capacity.

At first glance, these stories seem completely unrelated.

A President fighting for his nation’s survival
Targeted assassinations of defense executives
Sabotage across the cities of Europe
A high-stakes standoff in the Strait of Hormuz.

They aren't.

They're four stories about the same thing: Decision autonomy. Different actors. Different circumstances. Different outcomes. One framework.

What is Decision Autonomy?

Decision Autonomy is our individual and collective ability to accurately see the world around us, to trust the knowledge we have and the information we receive, and to make independent, confident decisions based on our own judgment. “I decide—we decide.” To be clear, this is about all of us—citizens, private sector leaders, military commanders and officials, and policymakers.

It’s not a perfect state, it isn’t binary, and it exists on a spectrum. Individuals, organizations, and nations are constantly moving along this spectrum—sometimes toward greater autonomy, and sometimes toward greater vulnerability to external pressure.

In the middle of that spectrum is Decision Malleability—a state in which decision autonomy becomes increasingly susceptible to external influences. We see reality less clearly, cognitive clarity erodes, judgment is increasingly influenced, and decisions are increasingly shaped by external pressures.

At the far end of that spectrum is Decision Compromise—a state in which external influences have displaced or constrained independent judgment, resulting in the loss of decision autonomy. Reality is distorted, cognitive clarity is lost, independent judgment is displaced, and decisions are no longer fully your own.

Our adversaries understand this. They don't have to completely compromise our decision-making to succeed. They simply have to move us toward greater decision malleability—just enough to delay a decision, divide an organization, increase uncertainty, create hesitation, or influence a false choice.

If we accept that the ultimate objective of cognitive warfare is to undermine, degrade, and compromise decision autonomy, then understanding what our adversaries are doing to achieve that goal is important. This battle—the battle for Decision Autonomy—is becoming the new front in strategic competition.

What external pressures are our adversaries using in this battle? There are many, but I want to focus on four primary pathways.

First—deception. Deception distorts our understanding of the world around us—reality itself—by persuading us that false realities are real, to doubt the truth we actually see, or simply misperceive the environment in which we are making decisions. What does deception sound like?

“Ukraine is run by Nazis.”

“We are not attacking you—we are protecting you.”

“They started it.”

“Joining NATO would be a hostile act.”

Second—manipulation. Manipulation influences our judgment by exploiting our emotions, identities, biases, and motivations, steering how we evaluate information and the decisions we make. Fear, anger, exhaustion, hopelessness, or hope can override deliberate reasoning. What does manipulation sound like?

“The West doesn’t respect who you are.”

“America will abandon you.”

“China offers a future that NATO can’t.”

“Why should those from outside the region tell you how to run your country?”

Third—coercion. Coercion constrains our freedom to choose by threatening or imposing unacceptable consequences if we do not make the decision our adversaries desire. The logic is simple: “you do X and we’ll respond forcefully.” What does coercion sound like?

“Join and we will take action.”

“Recognize Taiwan and there will be consequences.”

“Support our enemies and your interests will not be safe.”

“Advance our interests in the region or lose access to our markets.”

Fourth—cognitive overload. Cognitive overload overwhelms our ability to think clearly and rationally by exceeding our capacity to process information, evaluate competing narratives, and anticipate the consequences of our decisions. What does cognitive overload feel like?

“An endless stream of conflicting narratives.”

“One video says one thing—another says the opposite.”

“Experts disagree.”

“Anonymous sources contradict official sources.”

“Too many decisions, too much information, too little certainty, too little time.”

Our adversaries seek to create cognitive overload; our objective is to preserve cognitive clarity.

Cognitive clarity isn’t merely the absence of confusion. It’s the ability to remain intellectually focused, emotionally composed, and deliberately engaged despite uncertainty, complexity, competing information, information overload, and attempts to shape judgment.

In terms of these decision states, let’s test the framework against the five examples I opened with.

In Ukraine, President Zelensky and Ukraine maintained decision autonomy. They held firmly to reality, resisted deception, manipulation, and coercion, and made independent decisions despite extraordinary pressure. In this case, decision autonomy prevailed.

Russia’s assassination plots failed to remove key decision makers or undermine support for Ukraine. In fact, exposure of the plots appears to have had the opposite effect—hardening political resolve, increasing intelligence collaboration, strengthening protective measures around critical industrial leaders, and prompting defense companies to increase production. In this case, exposing Russia’s deception sharpened the view of reality and strengthened decision autonomy rather than degrading it.

Russia’s sabotage campaign has been heavy and costly. It is hard to assess if decision autonomy has been degraded. What is clear is that shared operational awareness has increased, defense collaboration is on the rise, an awareness that Russia favors Endless Warfare over peace is settling in, and a goal of shared strategic deterrence has emerged. If there’s a lesson here, it’s that an adversary can create enormous pressure without necessarily achieving decision compromise.

Iran’s disruption of the Strait of Hormuz has revealed the limitations of conventional military power against an adversary employing gray and asymmetric warfare methods. More importantly, it demonstrates how even a superpower finds its decision space constrained by a committed adversary.

The U.S. and its allies are moving along the decision continuum as they seek a decision to resolve this crisis. The question is whether this movement along the continuum reflects normal strategic decision-making under pressure—or a degradation of decision autonomy.

All these examples identify five key points that can protect decision autonomy:

Protect reality.
Seek evidence. Challenge assumptions. Verify before believing.

Preserve independent judgment.
Don't outsource your thinking to algorithms, echo chambers, crowds, or even experts that speak at conferences.

Maintain cognitive clarity.
Slow down. Reduce noise. Watch for fatigue, anger, urgency, despair, and overload.

Recognize and resist coercion.
“Am I choosing this—or am I being pressured into it?”

Continuously assess your decision autonomy.
Where am I on the continuum right now—autonomy, malleability, or compromise?

Is this relevant to the great power competition we all play a role in today?

Imagine these same pathways—deception, manipulation, coercion, and cognitive overload—employed deliberately and systematically by our adversaries over years or even decades, supported by intelligence services, state media, proxies, cyber capabilities, artificial intelligence, economic leverage, and military power. Scale changes everything.

Let’s talk about Russia, China, and Iran. All three countries use all four pathways, but each tends to emphasize them differently.

Russia has increasingly adopted a strategy of persistent confrontation with the West. It recognizes that it cannot match the United States, NATO, and its allies across every dimension of national power, so it competes asymmetrically and in the Gray Zone.

Russia seeks advantage by increasing uncertainty, delaying decisions, dividing alliances, employing proxies, and raising the perceived costs of action. It exploits negotiations to shift blame, abruptly change positions, and weaponize deception, delay, and distraction.

Russia understands that it doesn't have to defeat its adversaries militarily if it can influence their decisions before military force is ever employed. Deception and coercion define its approach.

Deception through disinformation, false narratives, active measures, and reflexive control.

Coercion through nuclear signaling, red lines, energy leverage, sabotage, assassination, and intimidation.

For China, patience is a strategic weapon. Rather than seeking to influence a single decision, China seeks to shape the long-term decision environment so that decisions favorable to Beijing gradually become the norm and ultimately viewed as being in the target's own interest.

As leading foreign policy expert Elizabeth Economy has observed, “China is executing a patient, multi-decade campaign to dominate the "new frontiers of power"—a continuous effort to set conditions, rewrite rules, and erode Western advantages below the threshold of open conflict.

Manipulation and coercion define this approach.”

Manipulation through United Front activities, influence operations, elite networks, and weaponized narratives.

Coercion through economic leverage, market access, technology dependence, sanctions, military expansion, and aggressive maritime tactics.

Iran views its struggle against the West as enduring and existential. Rather than seeking decisive military victory against stronger powers, it relies on persistent gray-zone competition, asymmetric warfare, and proxies to preserve regime security while constraining the decision of its adversaries.

Iran seeks to narrow the choices of the U.S. and its regional allies—"accommodate its interests or accept an unending and costly regional conflict.”

Manipulation and coercion define its approach.

Manipulation through ideological narratives, proxy media, and the exploitation of political divisions, sectarian identities, and regional instability.

Coercion through threats to global energy supplies, proxy violence, direct attacks on neighbors, hostage-taking, and terrorism.

Although their approaches differ, all three share a common objective: to shape how we perceive reality, exercise judgment, and ultimately make decisions that advance their interests over our own.

Of course, our adversaries still try to shape specific beliefs, but the longer-term payoff comes from shaping the conditions under which those beliefs form—to keep us consistently closer to Decision Malleability on issues most important to them.

So, what do we do about it? Let me close with what I believe are the human foundations of cognitive security—protecting cognition and decision autonomy.

This is often where we start talking about structural fixes—new organizations, whole-of-government approaches, media literacy, and technology. Some may be necessary; some remain aspirational. But I'd like to leave that conversation for another day and focus on the more human side of cognitive security: protecting cognition and decision autonomy.

Today, a clear view of reality can resemble a wilderness of mirrors—seeing isn't believing. If adversaries can replace facts with disinformation and synthetic realities, they gain a decision advantage.

Most of us have too many sources of information flooding our professional and private lives—I certainly do. It is easy to rely on so-called experts, chatbots, social media, comfortable echo chambers, and ubiquitous algorithms to do our thinking for us. It can become a blissful rut. When we knowingly or unknowingly cede judgment and decision space to others—we begin to lose decision autonomy.

We are living in a cognitive storm—a chaotic and unreliable global information environment where a single operator with a laptop can reach millions at the speed of global communications, where countless media sources are almost impossible to vet in real time, and where adversaries deploy AI-enabled networks of surrogates, fake sites, cybercriminals, hacktivists, and bots to target all of us and our institutions. It is easy to feel overwhelmed.

Russia, China, Iran, and even North Korea use redlines, threats and intimidation as tools of persuasion. The fear of escalation can be powerful, and our adversaries will seek to use coercion to move us along the continuum toward malleability and compromise. Coercion changes how we see the cost of our decisions and what we are willing to risk.

Our goal is to recognize coercion for what it is and not allow the fear of consequences—real or manufactured—to become the basis for our decisions.

We do have to accept certain things.

We cannot eliminate deception.

We cannot eliminate manipulation.

We cannot eliminate coercion.

We cannot eliminate cognitive overload.

But before making our most consequential decisions—in a military command post, a policy meeting, during a crisis, or in negotiations with our adversaries—we can stop—and ask four questions. I call this the Decision Autonomy Diagnostic: four questions to instantly evaluate where you stand on the continuum.

Do I accurately see and understand the world around me?

or - Do I know what’s true?

Am I evaluating the information objectively, or is something shaping my judgment?

or - Can I recognize manipulation?

Have I preserved cognitive clarity despite uncertainty, complexity, and overload?

or- Can I still think and deliberate clearly?

Can I decide independently despite external pressures?

or - Can I resist false threats and real pressure?

Finally, decision autonomy is ultimately about sovereignty. For nations, sovereignty is the freedom to determine their own future without external influence or interference—self-determination.

For individuals, decision autonomy is the expression of that same principle—personal sovereignty—the freedom to see reality clearly, exercise independent judgment, and make decisions that remain our own. Sovereignty gives us the right to decide. Decision Autonomy gives us the ability to decide.

No human capacity is more powerful—or more vulnerable—than our ability to make decisions—as individuals, as people, as nations—together, we must go to great lengths to protect it.

Can 'America First' survive Trump's war-first presidency?
item.description:
In a Thursday address at the GOP midterm convention that exalted President Donald Trump and demeaned his opponents as “extremists who openly hate our nation,” Vice President JD Vance hardly spoke about foreign policy.

He did not mention the war in Iran directly, and he only brought up foreign policy as an example of an issue that divides the party’s base. He urged voters not to “throw the baby out with the bathwater” because “you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there.”

The acknowledgement of foreign policy as a divisive issue in the MAGA coalition is a stark retreat for Vance, who staked his 2023 endorsement of Trump on the fact that “he started no wars despite enormous pressure from his own party and even members of his own administration,” framing the president’s America First record as a much-needed deviation from decades of bipartisan hawkishness.

A few wars later, Vance appears to have backed down from the anti-war aspects of the America First movement. Meanwhile, in response to the Iran war and the administration’s supposed betrayal of its campaign promises, the Institute for Peace & Diplomacy has launched “Reclaiming America First,” an initiative meant to take back that mantle from what it describes as Trump's hawkish drift, and to articulate an alternative vision for American foreign policy.

Arta Moeini, director of research at the Institute for Peace & Diplomacy and one of the project leads, laid out the parameters he believes should guide an “America First” approach during a Thursday panel marking the launch of the event: it should be neither ideological nor partisan, nor tied to any one individual; it should be grounded in realism; and it should prioritize core U.S. security interests and domestic renewal while rejecting unilateralism and nativism.

“Trump has shown himself to be at least disingenuous about using the term ‘America First,’” Moeini said during the panel, adding that part of the inspiration for the discussion was to combat “the taint of that association of ‘America First’ with this version of Trump.”

That question of who actually carries the tradition forward inevitably turned to Vance, long seen as its standard-bearer within the administration, but whose own words offer a measure of how far the movement’s foreign policy rhetoric has shifted since Trump’s return to office.

While panelists mostly agreed that an “America First” foreign policy was likely only to come from a conservative U.S. president, the group's read on Vance as the steward of that vision was more measured. Moeini said Vance would have been “smart enough not to go to war" with Iran, even if he might not be the right person to fix U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East.

Michael Brendan Dougherty, a senior writer for the National Review, offered a grimly ironic assessment of how a more realist foreign policy could take hold in a hypothetical Vance administration.

“If Vance is elected president after Donald Trump, he’s going to be looking at a munitions stockpile that is very depleted, and will be discouraging of him taking on unpredictable gambles. That’s not the way you want restraint to [be achieved], but it is the way it’s going now,” he said. “The Iran war is bringing about a humiliation of America, and that will bring along at least some restraint.”

Dougherty also pointed to the constraining effect of public opinion, saying that American opposition to war may have prevented Trump from taking even more dramatic steps in Iran, such as an invasion of Kharg Island.

There is evidence that elements of Trump’s base have turned against him as a result of this war. A recent survey from Navigator Research found that roughly 20% of Trump 2024 voters regret their decision. Among that group, almost half cited the war with Iran as the primary reason for their regret.

There were real policy disagreements over what "America First" meant. Daniel McCarthy, editor of Modern Age, warned that talk of a "multinodal" world echoes liberal internationalism and misreads an American public that is still proud of the country, while the panel also split over whether to encourage or deter a Polish or Japanese nuclear program. But all the panelists agreed that America First is a foreign policy movement that both predates and will outlive Trump.

“America First as an ordering principle of American statecraft will long outlive MAGA and the current coalitional dynamics at play surrounding the president,” Reid Smith, Vice President for Foreign Policy at Stand Together, said.

item.title: Call it the Miliband doctrine. Let’s hope the new Israeli settlement boycott is just the start | Steve Bloomfield
item.description:
This week’s move suggests that, even in the age of Trump, Britain will once again have an ‘ethical dimension’ to its foreign policy. That’s good for the world

Almost 30 years ago, the Labour titan Robin Cook announced his arrival at the Foreign Office by laying out what would become described as an “ethical foreign policy”. The UK, he said, “must support the demands of other peoples for the democratic rights on which we insist for ourselves”. Human rights would be “at the heart of our foreign policy”.

In the 25 years since Cook was demoted, Britain has had a further 14 foreign secretaries – including seven in the past six years – few of whom can claim to have placed progressive ideals at the heart of their actions. Ed Miliband’s speech on Tuesday outlining the UK’s decision to impose economic sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank – and unveiling the international coalition he has built to support it – suggests that Cook may finally have a successor.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer and a previous winner of the Orwell prize

item.title: Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon Tisdall
item.description:
The Russian leader is ploughing on with his forever war – and each day is a crime against humanity. Western democracies cannot simply sit on their hands

Ukraine’s people face a winter from hell. Thwarted on the battlefield, Russia is stepping up systematic, daily attacks on civilians, their homes, schools, hospitals, workplaces, and the vital infrastructure that sustains human life. Wave after wave of terrifying daytime ballistic missile and jet-drone strikes on Kyiv and other cities are destroying supermarket distribution hubs, pharmaceutical and medical facilities, logistics centres and warehouses. The result is sharply rising civilian casualties and growing shortages of food and other essentials. As a freezing winter approaches, Russia will again try to blow up Ukraine’s water supplies and power grid, cutting off electricity to millions. This is Vladimir Putin’s version of darkness at noon. He’d rather kill everybody than admit he’s lost.

Russia’s leader reportedly told Donald Trump this week that his “special military operation”, now in its fifth year, was going to plan. Trump may believe him. Western analysts certainly don’t. Failing militarily and taking huge casualties, his regime is under growing domestic economic and public pressure to wind down the war. Yet Putin seems to think one last big push can finally break Ukraine’s will. Trump’s renewed meddling – after months of inertia, he sent his patsy envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, back to Moscow last weekend (they also visited Kyiv for the first time) – perpetuates Kremlin delusions of victory. Now there’s talk of more talks. And all the while, Putin kills and kills. Each day is a crime against humanity.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

Against the odds, BRICS overcomes sharp divisions in New Delhi
item.description:
The 18th summit of BRICS, a grouping with ten members including Brazil, China, India, Indonesia, Russia, and South Africa, concluded in New Delhi with a leaders declaration — a clear success for an event that brought together a deeply divided group of countries, including some currently fighting on either side of a war in the Middle East.

Key world leaders attended, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, and Egyptian leader Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. There was, of course, the expected pageantry. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim even belted out a 1960s Bollywood hit at the leaders’ dinner party to the admiration of his Indian hosts.

This success was not guaranteed. Just a few months previously, BRICS foreign ministers had failed to agree to a joint statement amid acrimonious exchanges between Iran and the United Arab Emirates, which have exchanged missile barrages amid the ongoing war in the Middle East. Despite these serious rifts, host India managed to pull off a declaration that everyone signed on to.

The price of this success, however, was much-watered down language on the Middle East war. The summit declaration in Rio de Janeiro last year had come out swinging, stating that “we condemn the military strikes against the Islamic Republic of Iran since 13 June 2025, which constitute a violation of international law and the Charter of the United Nations.” In New Delhi this past weekend, the grouping merely expressed “deep concern over the continued escalation of tensions in Middle East/West Asia.” It recalled “our respective national positions” and called for “exercising maximum restraint, as well as avoiding actions that could further aggravate the situation.”

Admittedly, India’s task was tougher than Brazil’s had been, with the war having escalated since late February 2026 to include the UAE as a combatant. It is extremely difficult for a club to reach any sort of consensus if two of its members are physically brawling. From this perspective, the New Delhi declaration was a win for India. But it was more a relief than a victory for BRICS as a whole. The grouping did not need the distraction at this critical juncture in its journey.

Beyond the Iran-U.S. war, there were other notable aspects to the declaration. Mysteriously, all references to the Ukraine conflict were dropped. The European war had been consistently mentioned in BRICS declarations since Russia invaded in 2022. Last year, the text had even included language that largely reflected the Russian position on Ukrainian attacks on three sites.

One welcome new feature of the text was a paragraph on Cuba, expressing "deep concern" on the "tightening of unilateral blockade measures (and) their adverse effects on the Cuban economy...and the worrying humanitarian impact on the Cuban people.” U.S. pressure on Cuba has grown manifold since last year. Havana is now a “partner country” within BRICS, a lower tier of membership. The text was clearly a nod to its concerns. But feelings against the embargo and blockade against Cuba run high in the United Nations. Practically all member states have repeatedly gone on record opposing them.

Like last year, Israel was mentioned by name and criticized for its actions in Lebanon. The text also maintained the strong language on Gaza from earlier years. Concern was expressed at "arrangements that may prejudice the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people and legitimize or prolong occupation." There were no references to the U.S.-initiated "Board of Peace" in the text, even though BRICS states Egypt, Indonesia, and UAE are among its members, as are partner countries Kazakhstan and Vietnam.

Finally, the text expressed strong criticism of the “imposition of unilateral coercive measures that are contrary to international law,” emphasizing that “unilateral economic sanctions and secondary sanctions, have far-reaching negative implications for the human rights, including the rights to development, health and food security, of the general population of targeted states.” It further characterized such measures as “undermin(ing) international law and the principles and purposes of the UN Charter.” This language was a clear dig at the United States and its European allies. Many Global South states feel highly vulnerable to the U.S.-led global sanctions regime.

Having launched some successful initiatives like the New Development Bank, and with its major expansion phase now behind it, BRICS finds itself at a crossroads. The growing pains of expansion are manifest, and the outbreak of multiple wars in the world couldn’t have come at a worse time. It will take some time for new members to be adequately socialized in the grouping. Over the next year or two, BRICS will need to take a deep breath and find its footing again if it is not to lose its mojo.

item.title: Push to sanction Serbia could empower leader it aims to hurt
item.description:
On August 27, Reps. Joe Wilson (R-S.C.) and Bill Keating (D-Mass.) introduced the SRBIJA Act, which would impose sanctions and visa restrictions on “malign actors” accused of undermining democracy, the rule of law, human rights, and stability in the Western Balkans. The proposed legislation also threatens sanctions on Serbia if Belgrade maintains its relationships with Russia, China, and Iran.

The initiative comes as Serbia prepares for snap parliamentary elections next month, following nearly two years of anti-government protests and shortly after Washington and Belgrade launched a new Strategic Dialogue. In Serbia’s polarized political environment, supporters of President Aleksandar Vučić portray Wilson and Keating as hostile foreign actors seeking to dictate Belgrade’s foreign policy, while opponents of the government largely see the SRBIJA Act positively and hope it will “ultimately lead to [Vučić’s] downfall,” said Nikola Mikovic, a Serbian geopolitical analyst.

The SRBIJA Act’s sponsors hope their legislative push will pressure Belgrade to abandon its delicate balancing act between the West, Moscow, and Beijing. But the bill could instead give Vučić an opportunity to strengthen the geopolitical narrative that he has shrewdly navigated a multipolar world, which resonates with many Serbian voters and has helped keep him at the helm.

Engaging Belgrade pragmatically


The SRBIJA Act does not represent the Trump administration’s approach to Serbia, underscored by the newly established Strategic Dialogue. Launched in July, it provides an institutional framework for continued bilateral engagement and cooperation across areas including energy and economics. The Trump administration will not abandon that framework because of a single bill in Congress.

Vladimir Trapara, a Belgrade-based political analyst, said the congressional initiative “stands poor chances of success” and argued that its failure could, if anything, help boost the Serbian government’s popularity at home.

The handling of NIS — Serbia’s oil giant, in which a pair of Russian state-owned companies control a majority stake — illustrates the more complicated reality of Washington’s approach. The Trump administration has granted sanctions waivers to NIS while Belgrade works to resolve the company’s Russian ownership structure. On August 28, Serbia secured another U.S. waiver, giving the company additional time as negotiations continue over the potential sale of the Russian stake. In sum, the Trump administration continues engaging with Belgrade even while pressing Serbia’s government on issues where interests clash.

The Trump-Vučić relationship, meanwhile, has so far fallen short of the close personal partnership that some observers anticipated after Trump’s 2024 electoral victory. For all the talk of an autocratic affinity between the two leaders based on shared resentment of “globalists,” there is limited evidence that such a relationship has emerged.

“Vučić has quite desperately attempted to meet with Trump, even traveling to Mar-a-Lago to do so, and has always been thwarted in his efforts,” noted Lily Lynch, editor-in-chief of the Balkanist Magazine. Lynch explained that Serbia’s government has “settled into a pragmatic, if somewhat distrustful, relationship with the [second] Trump administration.”

Whatever expectations existed in Belgrade in late 2024 and early 2025 that the second Trump administration would dramatically shift U.S. policy toward the Western Balkans to align much more closely with Serbia, Washington’s approach has so far appeared more transactional. The region remains relevant to the United States because of energy, regional stability, Russia, China, Kosovo, and European integration, but those interests compete with a much wider set of priorities.

Ultimately, the Trump administration is simultaneously pressuring Belgrade and seeking to continue cooperation. Nothing suggests that Washington is preparing to abandon its relationship with Serbia. Consecutive administrations, going back at least as far as the 2000s, have seen U.S. engagement with Serbia as necessary for stability in the Western Balkans. Belgrade’s arms transfers to Ukraine and Israel have also helped insulate Serbia’s government from criticism from officials in Washington over its refusal to implement European sanctions on Russia.

Balancing the Great Powers


Congressional pressure is also unlikely to produce a dramatic pivot in Serbian foreign policy. Belgrade has already been incrementally moving closer to the West while maintaining its broader strategy of balancing among competing powers.

This is particularly visible in Serbia-Russia relations. Belgrade has maintained ties with Moscow while cooperating with Western governments and supporting Ukraine in ways that complicate its traditional relationship with Russia. Yet these developments have not amounted to Serbia abandoning its broader balancing strategy.

“Vučić is basically allowed by the West to retain this already low level of relations with Russia, in return for support to Ukraine and cooperation with the West on some other issues. On the other hand, Russia is happy to see [itself wield] at least this much…influence [as it does] in Serbia,” Trapara said. “This way, Vučić attracts support by both [the West and Moscow] for stability of his regime.”

China, which has emerged as Belgrade’s most important non-Western economic and strategic partner, presents a different challenge. Beijing’s presence in Serbia is primarily economic, making the relationship structurally different from Serbia’s ties with Moscow. Miković warned that a worsening U.S.-China confrontation could eventually put Belgrade under greater pressure to distance itself from Beijing — a potentially much more difficult decision for Vučić, who traveled to China in May 2026 and hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in May 2024.

Ultimately, Serbia has strong incentives to maintain relationships with the West, Russia, and China. Vučić has built considerable political capital around presenting himself as the leader capable of navigating between them.

Western pressure could strengthen Vučić at home


Besides Wilson and Keating, other Western policymakers seek to pressure Vučić’s government. Within the European Union, for which Serbia has been a formal candidate since March 2012, criticism has intensified over Serbia’s handling of the legacy of the 1990s Balkan wars. That issue has become particularly prominent following last month’s death of Ratko Mladić, the former Bosnian Serb military commander and convicted war criminal.

On September 3, a Serbian government plane flew Mladić’s body home to Serbia with his coffin wrapped in a Serbian flag. Days before Mladić’s funeral, held on September 7, EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a planned visit to Serbia, citing concerns about the glorification of Mladić, which Brussels warned “has no place in the EU or in EU candidate countries.” Just before the funeral, Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), and Rep. Keith Self (R-Texas) called on authorities in Belgrade to “refrain from any association with the planned ceremonies and to ensure that no public statement or official act memorializes Mladic as anything other than what he was: a convicted architect of genocide.”

For some of Vučić’s domestic supporters, criticism from Washington or Brussels reinforces perceptions that Serbia faces unfair pressure from the West. Since Slobodan Milošević’s ouster in 2000, “the issue of Serbian support for war crimes indictees and convicted war criminals has been a constant irritant to U.S.-Serbia relations,” said Lynch. That dynamic could become particularly relevant as Serbia approaches its parliamentary elections.

Western pressure could ultimately help Vučić with his core electorate. “Most of his voters have a strong focus on national issues, and they are likely to interpret this pressure as proof that Vucic is doing ‘a good job of defending Serbia’s interests,’ which is why those ‘evil Westerners’ want to overthrow him,” observed Miković.

Trapara stressed how much is at stake for Serbia’s elections in terms of democratic health, the rule of law, independent institutions, a free press, and constitutionalism. At the same time, he argued that outside actors should be cautious about intervening in Serbia’s domestic affairs.

“A message to the foreigners, whether they launch strategic dialogues in support of the regime, or fruitlessly threaten sanctions to help the regime anyway, is that they should refrain from big Serbia-related political moves until we finish our job in the elections.”

item.title: How to prevent another disastrous war in the 'in-between' states
item.description:
Only a few days ago, Moldova’s ambassador to the U.S. said it was likely “not an accident” that a Russian jet-powered drone flew across his country’s territory while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s plane was preparing to depart from Chișinău’s airport.

Armenia, meanwhile, continues to face Russian pressure over its increasing pro-Western orientation. And tensions continue to linger on Belarus’ western and southern borders following Ukrainian allegations this summer that the country is being used to advance Russia’s war effort.

Far from a disconnected smattering of events, these tensions stem from a larger regional crisis that predates — but was accelerated by — the Ukraine war. Bad U.S. policy played a crucial role in worsening this predicament.

In the decades following the end of the Cold War, the U.S. pursued a dual-track approach toward former Soviet states.

On the one hand, the West sought to integrate Russia — the strongest of all the new states and the USSR’s natural successor — as a junior partner into the U.S.-led liberal, capitalist world order. On the other, the U.S. and its European allies pursued a hedging policy across central and eastern Europe that included enlarging NATO up to Russia’s western borders, out of fear that Moscow’s historical autocratic and expansionist impulses would resurrect once more.

That dual policy “ultimately failed,” and the hedging “proved counterproductive,” as noted by Thomas Graham, one of America’s leading Russia scholars and practitioners. The Kremlin became convinced that America’s “true goal” was “eroding and containing Russian power,” a perception that drove Russia’s leaders to be “more determined to restore their might, push back against US initiatives in the former Soviet space, and drive wedges between NATO allies.”

Now that the post-Cold War unipolar era is definitively over, the U.S. must formulate a new policy toward the states stuck between NATO and Russia. This will be the key task — alongside preventing an escalation of the Ukraine war and rebalancing the trans-Atlantic relationship — for American policymakers focusing on Eurasia in the years ahead. The sum of these efforts will weigh upon two critical U.S. objectives: U.S. conventional retrenchment from Europe and the establishment of the conditions for long-term strategic stability between Russia and the West.

It was with these considerations in mind that we launched a Quincy Institute initiative focused on shaping U.S. policy toward Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, and Moldova — the so-called “in-between states.” In our newly-published inaugural report, we lay out a blueprint to help guide Washington’s policy toward this region in ways that will help advance America’s interests, support peace and prosperity, and avoid repeating the mistakes of the past.

A better approach to the in-between states would rely on a few key principles. One is that the U.S. has no vital interest at stake that necessitates it take on the risks of becoming a security guarantor for these countries. Another is that Washington should promote economic connectivity projects and political normalization efforts to strengthen Eurasian regional stability — and encourage in-between states to pursue multi-vector foreign policies that seek positive relations with all neighboring states.

Equally important here is the U.S. relationship with Russia. U.S. engagement in Eurasia must be accompanied by broader confidence-building measures with Russia, aimed at mitigating the risk of security spirals and misunderstandings.

This will require sustained dialogue with Moscow about what Washington is and is not doing, and the extent of its involvement in the in-between states. The Russians have demonstrated in both Georgia and Ukraine that they are willing to resort to the use of force to defend their interests in the in-between states, whereas NATO is not. The Kremlin has repeatedly made clear that it views the enlargement of the Western alliance into the in-between states as a red line.

It is, therefore, eminently sensible to take off the table the future expansion of NATO into former Soviet republics. Not only does it harm the foundations of Russia-West stability, but it also leads to greater instability for transatlantic partners and the in-between states themselves. When it comes to political and economic matters, however, the U.S. and the in-between states likely have greater room for maneuver.

In the context of the current security landscape, negotiating a compromise settlement to the Ukraine war will go a long way in assisting the U.S. with its other priorities across Eurasia and in the in-between states.

Washington’s greatest success to date in the in-between states is the August 8, 2025, announcement of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) at a White House ceremony with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, and President Donald Trump. Across Central Asia, the Caspian Basin, and the South Caucasus, American and European investments are increasing and political engagement is deepening. An important opportunity exists for TRIPP to become a key supply chain along the Middle Corridor, contributing to American efforts to strengthen U.S. access to the critical minerals essential to a modern economy and armed forces.

To ensure that this deepening engagement brings economic development and security to the South Caucasus, Washington must help Yerevan and Baku implement their peace agreement and facilitate normalization of Armenia-Turkey relations.

The Trump administration has achieved important successes through its engagement with Belarus, a country the U.S. had previously all but cast aside as an appendage to Russia. Pragmatic and consistent diplomatic work led to the release of several hundred political prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief. There remains much additional space for the development of political, diplomatic, and commercial ties between Washington and Minsk. A deliverable from a future potential meeting between Presidents Trump and Aleksandr Lukashenko may be full diplomatic normalization, which would open the door to increased trade and investment opportunities.

Final resolution of the remaining political-territorial disputes across the region — Transnistria in Moldova and Abkhazia and South Ossetia in Georgia — remains elusive. Nevertheless, a negotiated end to the Ukraine war alongside broader dialogue with Russia on European security matters would set the right conditions for progress in these other areas.

It’s high time for a new paradigm in the U.S. approach to the in-between states. Incorporating the strategic principles we lay out above into a new policy is vital to advancing American interests, fostering regional prosperity, and mitigating the risk of future crises in the Ukrainian mold.

item.title: How Trump's Iran operation turned into a forever war
item.description:
As the United States has struggled to secure its four primary objectives in the Iran War — achieving regime change, dismantling long-range ballistic missiles, eliminating nuclear enrichment, and halting Tehran’s support for regional proxies — U.S. officials have rolled out a series of tried-and-failed theories for how to achieve those goals.

In the past four weeks, Americans have watched their government attempt to inflict an economic victory against Iran through Operation Economic Outcast, tightening a sanctions regime which for decades has strangled Iran’s economy without resolving the underlying dispute.

Now, as that strategy flags, we have seen the Trump administration return to its older strategy of kinetic strikes against Iran. Those strikes, too, have failed to achieve their desired objectives.

Facing the prospect of a self-inflicted defeat, the U.S. has now proposed two new paths forward.

The first, reported by the Wall Street Journal last Wednesday, is an option to extend and formalize the current series of on-and-off strikes U.S. officials call this “mowing the lawn,” or a strategy of using periodic bouts of disproportionate force, as Israel did in Gaza prior to launching its full-scale, seemingly endless campaign after the Oct. 7 attacks of 2023. To support that option, the Pentagon has extended troop deployments in the Middle East through 2027.

The second option reportedly considered by the White House is for the U.S. to declare victory and walk away, with the Wall Street Journal reporting that Trump favors the idea. Among the supporters of the second option is Joe Kent, the former Director of the National Counterterrorism Center, who resigned in protest of the Iran War, and who has argued on X that the U.S. should “reset the terms of the deal” with Iran “by removing our troops & ships from the region.” The argument that the U.S should walk away and “declare victory” is growing increasingly popular even in establishment circles.

But given the historic limitations of sanctions to achieve political outcomes, coupled with Iran’s current demands, that strategy too appears unlikely to re-open the Strait of Hormuz and avert the economic consequences Iran’s leverage over the waterway will have on the global economy.

Political scientists have long doubted whether U.S. economic pressure and sanctions can shape political outcomes, particularly when the targeted state has little reason to believe these measures will be reversed in exchange for good behavior; researchers like David Siegel are quick to acknowledge that they “don’t work,” while U.S. officials like Janet Yellen have conceded the same point, noting that, while sanctions against Iran had caused a “real economic crisis,” they produced political outcomes “much less than we would ideally like.”

As Siegel — who most recently studied the failure of U.S. sanctions on Russia to redirect their state behavior toward U.S. and NATO interests — explains, “target states have strong incentives not to give in and sometimes even benefit from heightened levels of political support at home because they can now credibly blame their economic woes on a foreign imperial power.” Siegel argues that it's “probably more true today than ever before due to the fact that sanctioned states can turn to China.”

The low likelihood of economic pressure opening up the Strait of Hormuz is depressed even further by the fact that one of Iran’s preconditions for opening the Strait of Hormuz is the removal of sanctions, which would require a vote from Congress, where the proposal would face an uphill battle.

But perhaps the main reason walking away and declaring victory would fail to re-open the Strait and mitigate impending economic disaster is because Iran has tied freedom of navigation in the waterway to the U.S. reining in Israel, and the U.S. has long demonstrated it is unwilling to do so.

The June 17 agreement between the U.S. and Iran only required the U.S. force an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon, and Washington failed to follow through. Now, subsequent provocations by the U.S. and Israel have led Iran to expand its ceasefire demands to other campaigns: in Iraq, in Yemen, and in Palestine.

Securing a deal to re-open the Strait and end the war is further complicated by the growing view around the world that the “Art of The Deal” author is simply incapable of making deals. Results of a 2025 Politico survey of diplomats from 15 countries show foreign officials describing Trump’s deal-making process as “reactive, with no clear direction,” while Trump has so far failed to resolve a proxy war in Ukraine that he promised to end “within 24 hours” of taking office. The White House has similarly failed to reach a peace deal in Gaza.

Under these conditions, the broader Iran War appears to be rapidly approaching what a chief executive of a Danish shipping firm described to the Financial Times as a “Ukraine-style stalemate.” Speaking to the outlet in August, the CEO of Torn explained how “the Gulf leadership has realised they need to prepare themselves for a prolonged situation that lasts not days or weeks but months or years,” adding that “with the U.S. acting the way it is, I think it is a dream world to imagine the world returns to the way it was 10 years ago in the foreseeable future.”

The consequences of that “prolonged situation” will soon be felt even more by American consumers, as Iran’s control over the Strait of Hormuz has pushed diesel prices to their highest ever levels. Averting economic catastrophe will therefore require the U.S. to meet conditions it has so far been unwilling to accept; merely declaring victory and walking away won’t do the trick.

item.title: This Is Not Your Father’s Nuclear Flight Test Vehicle
item.description:
For decades, the United States’ nuclear weapons enterprise has wrestled with an institutional paradox. On one hand is the imperative to make the complex more “responsive” to global tumult and technical surprise, able to field new weapons quickly in reaction to unanticipated threats.
